sentences.speech: Build a three-lane tower-defense game in Scratch 3, then use its working parts to make another level.
This self-guided course is for advanced-beginner preteens: you know basic Scratch blocks, but lists, clones, and My Blocks can be new.
Build and test one small part at a time.
Build towers, defeat enemies, earn coins, and protect a base.
Use two short lists to keep track of six reusable shots.
Give clones their own lane and build-spot numbers.
Use My Blocks to keep useful tasks together.
Make a second level by changing settings instead of copying the game scripts.
Design, playtest, and explain a level of your own.
You can connect blocks, use repeat and if blocks, and create a variable.
You can rename sprites and draw or edit simple costumes.
You do not need previous experience with lists, clones, or My Blocks.
Use Scratch online at scratch.mit.edu in a desktop browser, signed in to your Scratch account.
You will not download or upload project files.
Work through the chapters in order in one Tower Defense project.
Choose File > Save now at each checkpoint.
To continue later, sign in, open My Stuff, and click See inside on your project.
Use the exact names shown for sprites, messages, variables, lists, costumes, and My Blocks.
Keep costumes centered and within the given sizes so the position checks match the artwork.
Use the green flag to restart the whole game.
lane
One horizontal road that enemies follow toward your base.
wave
A group of enemies that starts when the player clicks Start Wave.
level
A battlefield challenge containing one or more waves.
A new level starts with fresh towers, coins, and base health.
list
A numbered collection of values.
Item 1 in each shot list belongs to build spot 1.
My Block
A block you name and define for a useful task on one sprite or the Stage.
Calling it runs the blocks under its define block.
clone
A temporary copy of a sprite.
Variables made For this sprite only give each clone its own values.
game state
A value that says what the game is doing, such as ready, combat, or lost.
Scripts check it before acting.
update
One trip around the Stage's forever loop.
Towers, shots, and enemies each move once per update.
spawn
Make a new enemy appear at the start of its road.
The Stage does this with the Spawn Enemy message.
Enemies enter from the right.
Your base is on the left.
Towers beside each road shoot along it, but do not block enemies.
We will get one road working before expanding the game.
Sign in to Scratch and click Create.
Keep the Cat for now, because you will use it in the next step.
Type Tower Defense in the project title box at the top of the editor.
On paper, sketch three horizontal roads with a base on their left ends.
Mark two tower spots beside each road, near its left end: one above the road and one below it.
Next to your sketch, write what happens when an enemy is defeated: the player earns coins.
Write what happens when an enemy gets through: the base loses health.
A tower never needs its own health in this game.
Explain the route and the two possible outcomes for an enemy.
You can point to the entrance, base, and build spots and explain coins and base health.
Your sketch has three roads and six tower spots.
Enemies pass the towers rather than stopping to attack them.
Scratch uses numbers to say where a sprite is.
These numbers count pixels, the tiny dots that make up the screen.
The Stage is 480 pixels wide and 360 pixels high.
A 24-pixel Enemy is small: 20 of them fit side by side across the Stage.
Try the numbers with the Cat now, because every later step uses them.
Drag the Cat around the Stage and watch the x and y boxes under the Stage change.
Use those boxes to move the Cat to x 0, y 0.
The Cat jumps to the middle of the Stage.
Drag the Cat right, then left.
x gets bigger going right.
Left of the middle, x has a minus sign.
Drag the Cat up, then down.
y gets bigger going up.
Below the middle, y has a minus sign.
Use the y box to move the Cat to y negative 60, then to y negative 120.
The bigger the number after the minus sign, the lower the Cat goes.
Drag a change x by negative 2 block into the Code area and click it a few times.
x falls by 2 on each click, so the Cat moves 2 pixels to the left.
Your enemies will walk this way.
Delete that block, then delete the Cat by clicking the trash can on its thumbnail in the sprite list.
The edges of the Stage are x negative 240 on the left, x 240 on the right, y negative 180 at the bottom, and y 180 at the top.
Press Enter after you type in a box.
Without looking back, say where each of these is: x 0, y 0; x 220; x negative 210; and y negative 90.
Then say what change x by negative 2 does.
x 0, y 0 is the middle of the Stage.
x 220 is near the right edge.
x negative 210 is near the left edge.
y negative 90 is halfway down the lower half.
change x by negative 2 moves a sprite 2 pixels to the left.
You can explain what a minus sign means for x and for y.
You know that a bigger x means further right and a bigger y means higher up.
The Cat is deleted.
Every sprite uses the same x and y numbers to find places on the Stage.
The three road centers are y 90, y 0, and y negative 90.
The paint editor does not show coordinates, so you will paint Enemy first and use it as a guide while you draw.
We will use the top road first.
To make a new sprite, point at the cat button in the bottom right and click Paint.
Name the sprite Enemy in the Sprite box under the Stage, and name its costume Enemy.
Set the Outline number to 0 so an outline does not add to the size.
Paint a filled rectangle over the small center mark in the middle of the canvas.
A costume is centered when that mark is in the middle of the artwork.
Read the two numbers on the costume thumbnail, such as 24 x 20.
The first is the width and the second is the height.
Enemy must be no larger than 24 by 20.
If the shape is too big, select it with the arrow tool and drag a corner to shrink it.
Do not use the Size box under the Stage, because that does not change the costume's numbers.
Leave Size at 100.
Click the Stage in the bottom right of the editor, then click the Backdrops tab.
Rename the blank backdrop Battlefield.
Select Enemy and use the boxes under the Stage to move it to x 0, y 90.
Select the Stage.
On Battlefield, use the Rectangle tool to draw a road all the way across the backdrop, about as tall as Enemy.
Watch the Stage preview and make the road pass through the middle of Enemy.
Move Enemy to y 0 and draw the second road the same way.
Then move Enemy to y negative 90 and draw the third.
Move Enemy to x negative 210, y 0.
Use the Line tool to draw an up-and-down line through the middle of Enemy.
This is the base line, 30 pixels in from the left edge at x negative 240.
Leave the strips along the top and bottom of the backdrop empty.
Displays and buttons go there later.
Move Enemy to x 220, y 90.
This is where enemies enter, 20 pixels in from the right edge at x 240.
Check that its center sits on the top road.
Create Base Health and Game State with For all sprites.
Tick the checkboxes beside Base Health and Game State in the Variables list to show their displays.
Drag both displays to the top of the Stage so they do not cover a road.
A display covers whatever is under it, so keep every display in the top strip.
A click on a display does not reach the sprite underneath.
Use the zoom buttons below the paint canvas to draw tiny costumes more easily.
The enemy looks offset from its coordinates.
Select its artwork in Costumes and center it on the costume center mark.
Check that the sprite's Size box says 100.
Place Enemy at x 220, y 90.
The enemy is centered at the right end of the top road.
The three roads pass through y 90, y 0, and y negative 90.
The Enemy costume thumbnail shows no more than 24 x 20.
The Stage sends Enemy Step to ask Enemy to move once.
Each time the loop runs, Enemy moves 2 pixels to the left.
Using broadcast and wait lets that when I receive script finish before the Stage continues.
Later, the Stage will use this order to move shots before enemies check for hits.
On the Stage, add the green-flag script from the finished code section on this page.
Create the message Prepare Enemy from the first broadcast block's New message option.
Create Enemy Step from the broadcast inside the forever loop.
Use broadcast and wait for both messages.
On Enemy, add when I receive Prepare Enemy, followed by go to x: 220 y: 90 and show.
Add Enemy's when I receive Enemy Step script.
Put change x by negative 2 inside if Game State equals combat.
Inside that same if, after movement, add if x position less than negative 209.
The first x this is true for is x negative 210, the base line.
Inside this second if, put change Base Health by negative 1, set Game State to ready, and hide, in that order.
Click the green flag.
Wait for the enemy to reach the base, which takes about 15 seconds.
Check that health changes from 5 to 4 only once.
Game State is resetting during setup, combat while Enemy moves, and ready after it finishes.
The movement script checks for combat before acting.
Put the smaller if inside the larger if.
The outer check stops movement after Game State becomes ready.
The wait 0.03 seconds block is a short pause on each trip around the loop.
It belongs on the Stage, outside the if but inside forever.
Do not put forever under either Enemy message.
Health keeps dropping after the enemy disappears.
Set Game State to ready when the enemy escapes.
Keep movement and the escape check inside if Game State = combat.
Nothing moves.
Check that the Stage uses Enemy Step and the Enemy receives the same message.
Prepare Enemy must finish; it must not contain forever.
Watch one enemy escape, then wait a little longer.
Enemy hides at the base, Base Health stays at 4, and Game State says ready.
The enemy moves left smoothly.
Health drops once, not repeatedly.
Save a working version before adding towers.
Restarting during movement should give exactly the same starting position and health as the first run.
Click the green flag, then click it again while Enemy is halfway across the road.
Check that health returns to 5 and that the boxes under the Stage show Enemy back at x 220, y 90.
Let it escape and check that health remains at 4 afterward.
Choose File > Save now.
Click My Stuff at the top of the page, then click See inside on Tower Defense.
Repeat the escape test.
Compare both scripts with the finished code section on this page before continuing.
Reopening from My Stuff checks what Scratch actually saved, not just the project still open in the editor.
Restart keeps the enemy's old position.
Prepare Enemy must set both coordinates before show.
Keep the Stage's reset values above its forever loop.
Pass the restart and saved-project escape tests.
Every start resets health to 5; one escape leaves health at 4 in both the original and reopened project.
Both tests pass.
The project is saved and reopens from My Stuff.
One sprite can look like an empty build spot or a tower.
Its Built variable remembers which it is.
Looking at its costume is useful for the player, but the code will check the variable.
Continue in your Tower Defense project.
Paint a new sprite named Tower.
Give it a centered costume named Empty: a small, filled circle or square in a pale color, no larger than 28 by 24 pixels.
Set the Outline number to 0.
Keep the shape filled, because a click only counts on painted pixels.
The middle of a hollow shape cannot be clicked.
On the Costumes tab, point at the cat button at the bottom left and click Paint.
Name this second costume Built.
Make it a centered filled rectangle in a bold color, within the same 28 by 24 pixel limit.
Make Coins with For all sprites and tick its checkbox to show its display.
Drag the Coins display to the top-right of the Stage so it does not cover a build spot.
Select the Stage and the Battlefield backdrop.
Use the Text tool in the bottom strip, left of the middle, for the next two instructions.
Spots will sit near the left ends of the roads, so stay below the bottom road's lower spot.
Type this first line: Click an empty spot.
Tower: 30 coins.
Under it, type this second line: Need 30 coins; built spots cannot be bought again.
Select Tower.
Make Built with For this sprite only.
Its value will be 0 for empty and 1 for built.
Tick its checkbox to show its display.
Add Tower's Prepare Tower script from the finished code section on this page, creating that message in its event menu.
x negative 155 is near the left end of the road, and y 112 is 22 pixels above the top road at y 90.
A costume and a variable can both be named Built.
The costume controls appearance; the variable stores a number.
The spot appears on the road instead of beside it.
Use x negative 155 and y 112.
The top road is y 90, so this spot is 22 pixels above it.
Clicking the spot does nothing later on.
Fill the Empty shape so there are painted pixels in its middle.
Check that no display is covering the spot.
Click Tower's Prepare Tower script in the Code area.
An empty spot appears above the top lane and Built is 0.
The two costumes look different.
Built was made For this sprite only on Tower.
A My Block gives a task a name.
Try to build will check the rules, spend coins, and change the spot into a tower.
Keeping those blocks together makes the same task easy to reuse later.
Then the Stage will give the player coins and prepare the tower, so you can try it.
Select Tower, open My Blocks, and click Make a Block.
Name it Try to build with no inputs.
Tick Run without screen refresh and click OK.
Under define Try to build, add an if containing an or: Game State equals ready OR Game State equals combat.
Inside that if, add another if with an and block.
Put Built equals 0 in its left side.
Put a not block in the right side of the and.
Put Coins less than 30 inside the not.
not Coins less than 30 means 30 or more, so exactly 30 coins can still buy a tower.
Inside the inner if, change Coins by -30, set Built to 1, and switch costume to Built, in that order.
Add a separate when this sprite clicked script.
Attach the new Try to build block from the My Blocks category.
On the Stage, keep the existing green-flag script.
Insert set Coins to 90 after set Base Health to 5.
Insert broadcast Prepare Tower and wait after Prepare Enemy and wait, before Game State becomes combat.
Leave the movement loop unchanged.
The define block holds the task's blocks; the smaller Try to build block runs them.
The My Block belongs to Tower.
You will not find it in the Stage's My Blocks category.
Try to build has no loops or waits, so Scratch runs it all at once either way.
Ticking Run without screen refresh is a good habit for short My Blocks like this one.
Do not put a wait, glide, broadcast, or timed say block inside it.
The purchase works only with more than 30 coins.
Use not Coins less than 30, rather than Coins greater than 30.
Every click charges another 30 coins.
Keep the Built equals 0 check around the purchase.
Set Built to 1 immediately after taking away the coins.
Click the green flag and click the empty spot on the Stage once.
Coins goes from 90 to 60, the spot changes to the Built costume, and Built shows 1.
Both if blocks are nested as shown.
The click script uses the My Block rather than repeating its contents.
A useful test includes the edge of a rule.
Exactly 30 coins should work; 29 should not.
Clicking an occupied spot should never spend more coins.
Click the green flag and buy the tower.
Coins should change from 90 to 60; clicking it again should leave 60.
Restart without buying and wait until the enemy escapes, so Game State is ready and the tower is still empty.
For a temporary test, drag out set Coins to 29 from the Variables category into the Stage's Code area and click it.
Click the empty tower: it must stay empty with 29 coins.
Change the temporary block to set Coins to 30, click it, and try again.
The tower should appear and Coins should become 0.
Delete the temporary set block.
Restart and check that Coins returns to 90 and the spot is empty.
The tower does not shoot yet.
That is the next chapter.
Test both while the enemy moves and after it escapes: purchases are allowed in combat and ready.
The tower stays built after restart.
The Stage must broadcast Prepare Tower and wait before combat.
Tower must set Built to 0 and switch to Empty in its when I receive Prepare Tower script.
Pass the 29-coin, 30-coin, repeated-click, and restart tests.
Only an affordable first purchase changes coins.
Restart restores an empty spot and 90 coins.
Exactly 30 coins works.
A second click does not charge.
The temporary set block is deleted.
The game now has a purchase task that can be used by every tower spot later.
Enemy's code has not changed in this chapter.
Compare the Stage and Tower code in the finished code section on this page with your scripts.
Keep Enemy's complete Chapter 1 code.
Buy the tower during enemy movement, then restart and buy it after the enemy escapes.
Untick the Built checkbox in the Variables list so its display is gone from the Stage.
Choose File > Save now.
Reopen the project from My Stuff with See inside.
Repeat one purchase and a second click on the same spot.
Scratch also saves on its own, but File > Save now makes sure your latest change is saved before you test.
Clicking does nothing despite enough coins.
Click the spot on the Stage, not its thumbnail below the Stage.
Check that the sprite-clicked script calls Try to build.
Buy once in both allowed game states and repeat after reopening.
The first purchase leaves 60 coins, repeated clicks leave 60, and restart returns to 90.
The saved project passes the purchase tests.
You can explain why Try to build is a My Block.
Each tower will eventually have a numbered shot.
For now there is only shot 1.
Shot X stores its position.
Shot Active stores 1 while it is flying and 0 when it is available.
A list is like a variable with numbered items.
In Variables, click Make a List and create Shot X with For all sprites.
Create the list Shot Active with For all sprites too.
On the Stage, insert delete all of Shot X after set Game State to resetting.
Attach add 0 to Shot X immediately after it.
After those two blocks, attach delete all of Shot Active, followed by add 0 to Shot Active.
Tick the checkboxes beside both lists in the Variables list.
Click the green flag and check that each list shows exactly one item, numbered 1, with value 0.
Click the flag again.
Each list must still contain one item, not two.
Deleting the old items makes restart predictable.
Then untick both lists so their displays do not cover the Stage.
On Tower, create ID with For this sprite only.
Insert set ID to 1 immediately below Tower's when I receive Prepare Tower block.
Paint a sprite named Shot, with one costume named Shot: a filled, centered square, 6 by 6 pixels on its thumbnail, with the Outline number at 0.
About 80 of them would fit side by side across the Stage.
On Shot, create its own ID with For this sprite only.
On Shot, add when I receive Prepare Shot.
Create Prepare Shot in that event's menu, then attach set ID to 1 and hide.
On the Stage, insert broadcast Prepare Shot and wait after Prepare Tower and wait, before Game State becomes combat.
Click the green flag.
Select Tower and tick its ID checkbox, then select Shot and tick its ID checkbox.
Both displays should show 1.
Then untick both.
Both sprites have an ID variable, but they are separate because each was made For this sprite only.
Replace item changes an existing item.
Add makes the list longer.
Use add only during setup.
A list grows every time the flag is clicked.
Delete all of that list before adding its starting item.
Restart twice and check that each list still has one item with value 0.
Both lists have one zero, and Tower and Shot each have their own ID set to 1.
Both list lengths remain 1.
Shot is hidden after preparation.
Tower changes the list values.
Shot reads them and draws the shot.
This means the position used for hitting an enemy will be the same position used for showing the shot.
On Tower, make a My Block named Update my shot, with no inputs and Run without screen refresh selected.
Keep it short, with no waits or broadcasts.
Build the definition from the finished code section on this page.
Put every check inside if Built equals 1.
First, if this shot is active and its x position is greater than 230, replace its active item with 0.
x 230 is 10 pixels before the right edge.
The shot missed and can be reused.
Next, if its active item is 0, replace its x item with -135 and its active item with 1.
x negative 135 is the lane's firing point, 20 pixels to the right of the tower at x negative 155.
After those checks, replace its x item with its current value plus 10.
This moves the shot 10 pixels right on each update, including a newly launched shot.
Add when I receive Tower Step and call Update my shot.
Create Tower Step in that event menu.
On Shot, add the Draw Shots script from the finished code section on this page, creating Draw Shots in that event menu.
It reads the two lists, shows an active shot on y 90 during combat, and otherwise hides.
On the Stage, insert broadcast Tower Step and wait immediately before broadcast Enemy Step and wait, inside the combat if.
After the combat if, but before the 0.03-second wait, add broadcast Draw Shots and wait.
Restart and buy the tower.
At this step shots pass through enemies: watch a shot disappear near the right edge and a new shot begin at the firing point.
Drag Tower's round ID block into each item-number input.
Do not type the word ID into that input.
Put item ID of Shot X into the left side of the plus block, and type 10 on the right.
Keep Draw Shots outside the combat if so a final shot also hides when combat ends.
One update is one trip around the Stage's forever loop.
The shot never moves past its starting point.
Only launch when the active item is 0.
The final replace item must use the current x value plus 10, not just 10.
Nothing appears despite changing list values.
The Stage must send Draw Shots each loop.
Shot's ID must be 1 and Game State must be combat.
Watch a missed shot and its replacement before adding damage.
Only one shot is visible, and it travels from the left toward the right along the top road.
The lists stay one item long.
Tick them to check, then untick them.
A missed shot is reused.
Shots currently pass through the enemy; damage comes next.
A shot must count only once.
Enemy will mark it as used before taking damage.
We will put the check in a My Block with an input, so later we can ask the same block to check shot 1 or shot 2.
You will connect this block to Enemy Step two steps from now, so nothing changes on the Stage yet.
On Enemy, create HP with For this sprite only.
HP means the enemy's remaining health points; each enemy will need its own value.
Insert set HP to 2 immediately below when I receive Prepare Enemy.
Open My Blocks and click Make a Block.
Type Check shot as its name.
Click Add an input number or text and name the input slot.
Select Run without screen refresh and click OK.
As you build the definition from the finished code section on this page, drag the round slot input from its define block into each list item input.
Do not make a variable named slot.
Under define Check shot, add an if with HP greater than 0 as its condition.
Inside that if, add another if: item slot of Shot Active equals 1.
Inside that, add a third if.
Put an and block in its condition.
In the left side of the and, put a not block.
Inside it, build item slot of Shot X less than x position minus 12.
In the right side of the and, put another not block.
Inside it, build item slot of Shot X minus 10 greater than x position plus 14.
The next step explains these numbers.
Inside the position check, first replace item slot of Shot Active with 0, then change HP by -1.
Do not put a wait between them.
Slot is an input to this call, not a new shared variable.
A hit marks the shot inactive before another enemy could use it.
Hiding Shot by itself would not change the list.
If HP reaches 0, later calls do nothing, so a defeated enemy will not use another shot.
The input slot appears as plain text inside a list block.
Drag the rounded slot block out of the define block and into the item-number input.
Think through what Check shot 1 does when a shot hits.
Shot Active item 1 changes to 0 before HP falls from 2 to 1.
The input is a round block, not typed text.
The shot is marked used before damage.
No wait or broadcast is inside this definition.
One update is one trip around the Stage's forever loop.
In one update, the enemy moves left 2 pixels and the shot moves right 10.
They can cross between two drawn positions.
Our comparisons check that movement using the shot's center and an enemy half-width of 12.
On paper, draw an enemy center at x 100.
Its current left edge is 88, because 100 minus 12 is 88.
Write its previous center at 102.
Its previous right edge was 114: 102 plus 12.
Try a shot whose current x is 90.
Its previous x was 80.
The current shot is not left of 88, and its previous position is not right of 114: a hit.
Try a shot whose current x is 70.
It has not reached 88 yet: no hit.
Try a shot whose current x is 130.
Its previous x was 120, already beyond 114: no hit.
Match the numbers in your Check shot block: 12 is the enemy's half-width, 10 is how far the shot moved this update, and 14 is 12 plus the 2 pixels the enemy moved this update.
Keep the movement speeds fixed in this course.
Now draw two enemies overlapping at x 100, each with HP 2.
Give shot 1 an x value of 90 and an active value of 1.
Work through the first enemy's Check shot 1: the position check passes, Shot Active item 1 becomes 0, then that enemy's HP becomes 1.
Work through the other enemy's Check shot 1: the active item is already 0, so its HP stays 2.
One shot caused only one hit.
Scratch may check either enemy first; our game does not promise which one.
The Sensing block touching Shot checks whether the costumes touch at their current positions.
This game uses the positions in Shot X instead, so it can check a crossing between moves before Shot draws its new position.
Not less than includes equality.
Not greater than also includes equality.
You are checking a small movement that happened during this update, not searching the whole road for an enemy.
Every enemy is hit as soon as a shot appears.
The two comparisons must be joined by and, not or.
Check the nesting of not and each comparison against the finished code section on this page.
Explain the three shot examples using your drawing.
Shot x 90 hits the enemy at 100; shots at 70 and 130 do not.
You can point to the current and previous shot positions.
You have kept shot movement at 10 and enemy movement at -2.
Enemy now uses its HP to decide whether it was defeated.
A defeated enemy earns coins.
An escaped enemy damages the base.
Only one of those outcomes should happen.
On Enemy, replace the earlier Enemy Step script with the version in the finished code section on this page.
Keep Prepare Enemy and the Check shot definition.
After moving left by 2, add a Check shot block with input 1.
Add an if block with an else space, with HP less than 1 as its condition.
In its top space, add 10 coins, set Game State to ready, and hide.
In the else space, put the original escape check.
It still removes one base health, sets ready, and hides.
If the HP display is not on the Stage, select Enemy and tick the checkbox next to HP in the Variables category.
Restart and buy the tower in the first few seconds.
Watch HP reach 1 after one hit and 0 after the next.
Coins should go from 90 to 60 to 70.
Wait after the enemy disappears.
Coins must stay at 70 and base health at 5.
Restart without buying.
The enemy should escape, leaving 90 coins and 4 base health.
Defeat and escape each get their own space in the if block.
Do not put the escape test after the whole block.
Once Game State becomes ready, the Stage stops sending movement and attack messages, but still sends Draw Shots to hide the last shot.
Coins keep increasing after a defeat.
Set Game State to ready in the top space of the HP less than 1 block.
Keep the entire Enemy Step inside if Game State equals combat.
Test one defended run and one undefended run.
Defense ends with 70 coins and 5 health.
No tower ends with 90 coins and 4 health.
Each enemy takes two hits.
Only the defeat awards coins.
Neither outcome repeats afterward.
You now have a working purchase, shot, and enemy.
The next chapter will number more copies instead of inventing six different shooting scripts.
Check the Stage's complete loop in the finished code section on this page.
Tower Step must finish before Enemy Step, followed by Draw Shots.
Check that Tower has its purchase code from Chapter 2, plus its new Update my shot definition and when I receive Tower Step script.
Prepare Tower must now also set ID to 1.
Check that Enemy has Prepare Enemy with HP 2, the Check shot definition, and only the replacement Enemy Step from this chapter.
Check that Shot has its Prepare Shot and Draw Shots scripts.
Untick both lists and HP in the Variables list, so their displays do not cover the playfield.
Choose File > Save now, reopen the project from My Stuff with See inside, and repeat the defended and undefended runs.
Restart while a shot is flying.
Both lists should reset to one item and the tower should return to Empty.
Tick the lists to check, then untick them.
Lists store the shot's facts.
Shot's show and hide blocks only draw those facts.
An old shot remains after restart.
Both lists must be cleared and given a zero during Stage setup.
Prepare Shot hides the sprite before combat begins.
Pass the saved-project attack, escape, and restart tests.
One tower uses one shot repeatedly, defeat awards exactly 10 coins, and restarting removes the old shot.
The saved project passes both outcomes.
The lists have exactly one item each after every restart.
No old movement script remains alongside its replacement.
A clone is a copy of a sprite that Scratch makes while the project runs.
When a clone is made, it copies the sprite's For this sprite only variables at that moment.
This short test shows that rule on a throwaway sprite before you use it for six tower spots.
Each copy keeps the number the original had when the copy was made, even though the original changes it afterward and ends at 0.
Paint a small new sprite named Clone Test.
Any simple shape works.
On Clone Test, make a variable named My Number with For this sprite only.
Build the green-flag script from the finished code section on this page.
create clone of myself is in the Control category.
Three times, the script sets My Number, moves, and creates a clone.
At the end it sets My Number back to 0.
Add when I start as a clone, then show and say My Number.
Click the green flag.
Three copies appear in a row, left, middle, and right, saying 1, 2, and 3.
Click the green flag again.
There are still exactly three copies, because Scratch deletes all clones when the green flag is clicked.
Right-click Clone Test in the sprite list and choose delete before you continue.
A clone runs when I start as a clone scripts.
It does not run when green flag clicked scripts.
Make spot in this chapter uses the same pattern: set the values, create the clone, then change the original's values again.
All three copies say 0.
Make My Number with For this sprite only, not For all sprites.
A shared variable is 0 by the time the copies speak.
Put each set My Number block before its create clone of myself block.
